summary: This document specifies fault management for Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links (TRILL) Operations, Administration, and Maintenance. It follows the IEEE 802.1 Connectivity Fault Management framework and reuses parts of it.

plainLanguage.summary: TRILL is the protocol that moves Ethernet frames between switches in one campus. This RFC says how to find out when a path through that network has broken. It builds on the fault management rules of the IEEE 802.1 standard, so most messages and checks are reused, and adds the parts that TRILL needs because its traffic can take several different routes at once.

subtitle: How a TRILL network finds the break when a path through it fails.

tldr.problem: A TRILL network forwards Ethernet frames between switches, and each switch picks among several equal-cost paths. When something fails, an operator has to find out which path broke and where, and the original TRILL specification had no way to identify monitoring frames at all.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines how TRILL switches exchange Operations, Administration and Maintenance (OAM) messages, reusing the IEEE 802.1 Connectivity Fault Management framework. A monitoring frame is marked with an Alert flag in the TRILL header and the CFM Ethertype, and carries a 96-byte Flow Entropy field so that it travels the same path as the traffic it is checking.
tldr.outcome: Loopback, path trace, multicast tree verification and continuity check messages now let an operator find a break, plot a path and see which flow failed. The document also defines a Base Mode that works with no configuration, and it updates RFC 6325 with the methods for identifying OAM frames.

facts.label: TRILL Header size
facts.value: 6 bytes when the Extended Header is absent

today: RFC 7455 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2015. It updates RFC 6325 to add the methods for identifying TRILL OAM frames, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or further updates it. Performance monitoring for TRILL is a separate document, RFC 7456, and the OAM framework it builds on is RFC 7174.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
TRILL forwards Ethernet frames between switches, and those switches are also known as RBridges or Routing Bridges. This document specifies the fault management for TRILL: how an operator finds out that a path through the TRILL campus has broken, and where it broke. Its methods follow the Connectivity Fault Management (CFM) framework defined in IEEE 802.1 and reuse the OAM tools defined there where possible. Additional messages and TLVs are defined for TRILL-specific applications and for cases where CFM needs a different set of information.

The document updates RFC 6325 by adding specific methods for identifying TRILL OAM frames, which the original TRILL specification did not have. Performance monitoring for TRILL is specified separately in RFC 7456. The high-level format of TRILL OAM messages is presented in RFC 7174, and this document fills in the details of the frame format.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC says how to find out when a path through a TRILL network has broken. It builds on the fault management rules that the IEEE 802.1 standard already defines, so most of the messages and checks are reused rather than reinvented.

sections.title: The Shape of a TRILL OAM Message
sections.content:
A TRILL OAM message has six parts. The Link Header is media dependent; for Ethernet it holds the destination and source MAC addresses, an optional VLAN, and the Ethertype fields. The TRILL Header is a fixed size of 6 bytes when the Extended Header is not included. The Flow Entropy is a 96-byte, fixed-size field whose rightmost bits MUST be padded with zeros when the flow-entropy information is shorter than 96 bytes; it enables emulation of the forwarding behaviour of the data packets being probed, and it starts with the Inner.MacDA. The OAM Ethertype is a 16-bit Ethertype that identifies the OAM Message Channel that follows, and this document specifies the Ethertype 0x8902 allocated for CFM. The OAM Message Channel is a variable-size section that carries OAM-related information, in the format defined in IEEE 802.1. The Link Trailer is media dependent; for Ethernet it is the Frame Check Sequence.

For accurate monitoring and diagnostics, OAM messages are required to follow the same path as the corresponding data packets. That is what the Flow Entropy field is for. It carries the information a switch would use to pick a path, so the probe is forwarded along the route the real traffic takes.
sections.plainLanguage: A monitoring message copies the shape of a normal TRILL packet. It carries the same 96-byte block of information that switches use to choose a route, so the monitoring traffic travels along the same path as the traffic it is checking.

sections.title: Marking a Frame as OAM
sections.content:
TRILL as originally specified had no flag or method to identify OAM frames. This document updates RFC 6325 to add one: the reserved bit next to the Version field in the TRILL Header becomes the Alert flag, denoted "A". RBridges MUST NOT use the flag for forwarding decisions such as choosing which equal-cost path or multi-destination tree to select. Implementations that comply with this document MUST use the flag together with the CFM Ethertype to identify TRILL OAM frames.

The value 1 in the flag means the frame may qualify as an OAM frame. Implementations are further REQUIRED to check that the value at the OAM Ethertype location is the CFM Ethertype 0x8902. If it matches, the frame is a TRILL OAM frame and SHOULD be processed as set out in Section 4. A frame with the flag set that does not carry the CFM Ethertype is not an OAM frame and MUST be silently discarded. OAM-capable RBridges MUST NOT generate OAM frames to an RBridge that is not OAM capable, and intermediate RBridges that do not understand the flag forward OAM frames with it unaltered.

Capability is announced with two flags in the TRILL Version sub-TLV: O for OAM capable and B for backwards-compatible OAM. With O set to 1 and B set to 0 the announcing RBridge uses the method of Section 3.2. With both set to 1 it uses the backwards-compatibility method of Appendix A. When O is 0 the announcing implementation is considered not capable of OAM, and the B flag is ignored. Absence of the TRILL-VER sub-TLV means the announcing RBridge is not OAM capable.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a switch can send monitoring messages, it marks them with a single bit in the TRILL header and with the EtherType that says what the message is. The receiving switch checks both, so an ordinary data packet that happens to set the bit is thrown away instead of being mistaken for a probe.

sections.title: Addressing Maintenance Points
sections.content:
In IEEE CFM, OAM messages address the target Maintenance End Point (MEP) with a unique MAC address. In TRILL a MEP is addressed by a combination of the egress RBridge nickname and the Inner.VLAN or fine-grained label. MEPs also carry a 2-octet MEP-ID that is independent of the underlying technology. In CFM the MEP-ID is restricted to the range 1 to 8191, but on the wire MEP-IDs are encoded in a 2-octet field, and in the TRILL Base Mode operation of Appendix B the MEP-IDs are mapped one-to-one with the RBridge nicknames. In TRILL a MEP-ID MUST therefore be a number from 1 to 65535.

At the MEP, OAM packets pass through a hierarchy of demultiplexers. First, the packets that need local processing are identified, and the MEP associated with the Inner.VLAN or fine-grained label is found. The MEP then validates the Maintenance Domain Level: a packet whose level is below the level of the MEP is discarded, a packet at the same level goes on to the OpCode demultiplexer, and a packet at a higher level goes to the next higher level demultiplexer if one exists, or is forwarded as normal data if none does. The OpCode demultiplexer then routes the packet to the right processor, and a packet with an unknown OpCode is discarded.

Maintenance Intermediate Points (MIPs) are mainly used for fault isolation. Any MIP in the ingress interface may reply to an incoming Path Trace Message, and the Sender ID TLV together with the Reply Ingress TLV identifies the responder uniquely. Because path tracing relies on a Hop Count expiry approach similar to the IP trace-route command, explicit addressing of MIPs is not required. On edge interfaces, MEPs MUST be configured to prevent TRILL OAM packets leaking out of the TRILL campus.
sections.plainLanguage: A TRILL switch is named by a short nickname rather than a hardware address, so monitoring messages are addressed by the nickname of the switch they are for plus the label of the traffic they describe. Each switch then sorts incoming messages by maintenance level and by message type, and discards anything it does not recognise.

sections.title: The OAM Message Header and Its TLVs
sections.content:
The OAM Message Channel has two parts: the message header and the TLVs. Every OAM message MUST contain a single header and a set of one or more TLVs. The header reuses the IEEE 802.1 layout and holds a 3-bit Maintenance Domain Level, a 5-bit Version, an 8-bit OpCode, a 1-byte Flags field whose meaning depends on the OpCode, and a 1-byte FirstTLVOffset giving the location of the first TLV. The remainder of the header may hold OpCode-specific information such as a session identification number and a timestamp.

Four TRILL-specific OpCodes are defined: 64 for Path Trace Reply, 65 for Path Trace Message, 66 for Multi-destination Tree Verification Reply and 67 for Multi-destination Tree Verification Message. Loopback and Continuity Check messages reuse the OpCodes defined in IEEE 802.1.

Each TLV has a 1-octet Type, a 2-octet Length giving the length of the value in octets, and a value whose content depends on the type. Eleven TRILL OAM TLVs are defined, numbered 64 to 74: the TRILL OAM Application Identifier TLV, the Out-of-Band Reply Address TLV, the Diagnostic Label TLV, the Original Data Payload TLV, the RBridge Scope TLV, the Previous RBridge Nickname TLV, the Next-Hop RBridge List TLV, the Multicast Receiver Port Count TLV, the Flow Identifier TLV, the Reflector Entropy TLV and the Authentication TLV. The Application Identifier TLV MUST be the first TLV in every message, and a message that does not include it as the first TLV MUST be discarded. An End TLV (0) MUST be included as the last TLV, and all other TLVs may appear in any order.
sections.plainLanguage: Each monitoring message starts with a short header that says what kind of message it is, followed by a list of information blocks called TLVs. One block must always come first, and it says what the message is for, including whether a reply is wanted and whether the label on the packet matched the one the sender expected.

sections.title: Loopback, Path Trace and Tree Verification
sections.content:
The Loopback Message asks one RBridge to confirm that it received a frame and can send a reply back. The request carries a 32-bit Loopback Transaction Identifier, also called the session identification number, which the responding RBridge MUST echo unchanged, and the reply sets the OpCode to 2. The originator identifies the destination nickname, builds the Flow Entropy, includes the TRILL OAM Application Identifier TLV and, where applicable, the Out-of-Band Reply Address, Diagnostic Label and Sender ID TLVs, sets the Hop Count, and dispatches the frame. It may retransmit at periodic intervals until a response arrives or the retransmission count expires, incrementing the session identification number each time. Intermediate RBridges forward the request as ordinary data frames.

The Path Trace Message has the same format and exists because the IEEE 802.1 Link Trace Message relies on a well-known multicast MAC address, which works in 802.1Q because the unicast and multicast paths are the same. In TRILL they are not, so TRILL uses a new message format. The originator sends it with a Hop Count of 1 and expects an "Intermediate RBridge" sub-code from the next hop or a "Valid response" from the destination. On receiving the intermediate reply it records the nickname and interface information of the node that answered and resends the message with the Hop Count increased by one. This continues until the destination answers, the process times out, or the Hop Count reaches a configured maximum.

The Multi-destination Tree Verification Message checks that a multicast distribution tree is intact and has not been pruned. It is copied to the processor of every intermediate RBridge in the tree being verified. The originator may name the RBridges that are in scope in an RBridge Scope TLV, and only those answer; the others discard the request silently. Inclusion of the scope field is required to prevent an excessive number of replies. Each scope TLV can hold up to 255 nicknames, and a message may carry several of them. When rate limiting or congestion causes an intermediate RBridge to discard the message, the requester has to retransmit, narrowing the scope to the RBridges that have not answered.
sections.plainLanguage: Three probes do the work. A loopback asks one switch to prove it can send a reply. A path trace walks the route one hop at a time, counting the hops, until it reaches the far end or times out. A tree verification asks every switch on a multicast route to confirm it still has the traffic, so a wrongly pruned branch shows up.

sections.title: Continuous Checking and Error Notification
sections.content:
Continuity Check Messages (CCMs) monitor connectivity and configuration errors. A MEP listens for periodic CCMs from its remote partners and spots a cross-connect error by comparing the MAID in the received CCM with its own. CCMs are unidirectional and have no explicit reply; each MEP reports its local status by setting the Remote Defect Indication (RDI) flag on the CCMs it transmits, and a MEP may raise SNMP traps as alarms when a connectivity failure occurs.

TRILL forwards packets over several equal-cost paths, so the path a packet takes depends on its payload. The Maintenance Association identifies the MEPs of a monitored path, and the entropy values of the monitored flows are defined within that association, so the CCM transmit logic builds its packets with the Flow Entropy of the flow being watched. The RFC therefore monitors connectivity per flow, and cross-connect errors per flow.

Each MEP transmits four CCM messages per flow, and the CCM timeout is three CCM intervals, so a fault is detected when three consecutive messages are lost. Every CCM has a unique sequence number and a unique flow identifier, and the flow identifier travels in the Flow Identifier TLV. When a MEP notices a timeout from a remote MEP it sets the RDI flag on its next CCM, and it logs and sends an SNMP notification carrying the remote MEP identification, the flow identifier and the sequence number of the last CCM it received. The RFC works through an example with two MEPs and three flows, where MEP-B receives sequence numbers 1 to 4 but not 5 to 8, detects the fault on the eighth message, and reports the last good flow identifier and sequence number. When a new CCM arrives after a timeout, the OAM sends a CCM resume notification with the first valid flow identifier and the sequence number after the timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: Two switches that watch each other send a short message every so often. If three of these messages in a row go missing, the switch raises an alarm. Because a TRILL network can send the same traffic along several different routes, each watch is tied to one flow, and the alarm says which flow failed and when the last message arrived.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Forged OAM packets could cause false error or failure indications, mask real errors, or be used for denial of service. Source addresses for messages can be forged, and the out-of-band reply facility provides for supplying the address for replies explicitly. The Authentication TLV can be used in a TRILL OAM message to protect against forged packets. It is virtually identical to the IS-IS Authentication TLV and depends on IS-IS keying material and the current state of IS-IS keying; there is currently no standardized IS-IS automated key management.

Authentication is ineffective unless it is verified, and it does nothing against a sender who holds the keying material. Implementations MUST implement rate-limiting to protect against OAM messages being used as a denial-of-service vector, although aggressive rate limiting may cause false positive errors against CCM and LBM session monitoring. Even with authentication, replay may be possible. Each of the four message types carries a field that can be used for replay protection: CCM messages carry sequence numbers, and Loopback, Path Trace and tree verification messages carry an identifier that is incremented with each transmission.

The MD-Level is embedded deep in the OAM message, so conventional frame filtering may not be able to filter on it, and messages that must be dropped because of an MD-Level mismatch may leak into a TRILL domain with a different level. This causes no loss of functionality, because the receiving MEP or MIP validates the MD-Level before acting on the message. Generally a single operator manages each TRILL campus, so there is no risk of security exposure, but in multi-operator deployments operators should be aware of possible exposure of device-specific information.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone on the network can send a fake monitoring message, so the RFC provides an optional block that lets a receiver check who sent it. It also insists that switches rate-limit monitoring traffic, because a flood of probes is itself a way to knock a switch over.

items.label: Path Trace Reply
items.desc: The answer to a Path Trace Message.

items.label: Path Trace Message
items.desc: Asks each hop along a path to identify itself.

items.label: Tree Verification Reply
items.desc: The answer to a Multi-destination Tree Verification Message.

items.label: Tree Verification Message
items.desc: Asks the switches on a multicast tree to confirm they still have the traffic.

viz.caption: THE ELEVEN TRILL OAM TLV TYPES

items.label: Application Identifier
items.desc: Must be the first TLV. Carries the version, fragment number, return code and the F, C, O and I flags.

items.label: Out-of-Band Reply Address
items.desc: The address an out-of-band reply must be sent to.

items.label: Diagnostic Label
items.desc: The VLAN or fine-grained label the message was generated in.

items.label: Original Data Payload
items.desc: The received TRILL header and flow entropy, echoed back in replies.

items.label: RBridge Scope
items.desc: The RBridges asked to answer a tree verification request.

items.label: Previous RBridge Nickname
items.desc: The nickname of the RBridge before the one replying.

items.label: Next-Hop RBridge List
items.desc: The equal-cost next hops on the way to the destination.

items.label: Multicast Receiver Port Count
items.desc: How many ports want the multicast stream.

items.label: Flow Identifier
items.desc: Names the flow being watched, together with the MEP-ID.

items.label: Reflector Entropy
items.desc: The flow entropy the responder must use in its reply.

items.label: Authentication
items.desc: Optional authentication of the message, using the IS-IS authentication type.

viz.caption: A PATH TRACE WALKING THE ROUTE ONE HOP AT A TIME

messages.label: PATH TRACE MESSAGE
messages.note: First transmission, sent with a hop count of 1.

messages.label: PATH TRACE REPLY
messages.note: Return sub-code 2, intermediate RBridge. The reply names the hop and its interface.

messages.label: PATH TRACE MESSAGE
messages.note: Resent with the hop count raised by one.

messages.label: PATH TRACE MESSAGE
messages.note: Resent with the hop count raised again.

messages.label: PATH TRACE REPLY
messages.note: Return sub-code 0, valid response. The path is complete.

viz.caption: HOW A CONTINUITY FAULT REACHES THE OPERATOR

items.title: Three lost messages
items.text: The fault is declared after three continuity check messages in a row go missing.

items.title: RDI flag
items.text: Set on the next continuity check message to say the far end has a fault.

items.title: Flow Identifier TLV
items.text: Names the flow being watched, so the alarm points at one route.

items.title: Sequence numbers
items.text: Each continuity check message carries one, so the receiver can see what it has missed.

items.title: SNMP notification
items.text: The alarm itself, carrying the remote MEP, the flow identifier and the last sequence number received.
